ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: TRALI is an acute, non‑cardiogenic lung injury occurring within 6 hours of a blood product transfusion, caused mainly by donor anti‑HLA antibodies. It mimics pneumonia but resolves with supportive care.

sections.p: TRALI is an acute lung injury that develops during or within 6 hours after transfusion of blood components, characterized by hypoxemia, bilateral pulmonary infiltrates, and no evidence of circulatory overload.
b: Diagnostic criteria: acute onset, PaO2/FiO2 ≤ 300 mmHg, bilateral infiltrates, no left atrial hypertension, onset ≤ 6 h after transfusion.

sections.p: Severity is graded by the degree of hypoxemia and need for respiratory support, using the Berlin ARDS criteria adapted for transfusion timing.
b: Mild: PaO2/FiO2 200‑300 mmHg, supplemental O2 only.
Moderate: PaO2/FiO2 100‑200 mmHg, non‑invasive ventilation.
Severe: PaO2/FiO2 < 100 mmHg, invasive ventilation.

sections.p: Most cases are antibody‑mediated, but a second “two‑hit” mechanism (patient neutrophil priming) also contributes.
b: Donor anti‑HLA or anti‑HNA antibodies (especially from multiparous women).
Biologically active lipids accumulating in stored blood.
Patient factors: infection, surgery, massive inflammation, malaria, HIV, sickle‑cell crisis.

sections.p: Patients develop sudden dyspnea, cough, fever, and tachypnea, often with pink frothy sputum, while blood pressure may stay normal or fall.
b: Rapid onset (minutes‑hours) after transfusion.
Bilateral crackles, no peripheral edema.

sections.p: Investigations confirm non‑cardiogenic edema and rule out other causes.

t.b: Does the patient have bilateral infiltrates? Positive supports TRALI; normal film argues against.
What is the PaO2/FiO2 ratio? ≤ 300 mmHg meets criteria; higher values suggest milder injury.
Is cardiac overload present? Low levels favor TRALI; high levels suggest TACO.

t.a: Donor plasma testing for anti‑HLA/HNA antibodies
t.b: Is an antibody present? Positive confirms antibody‑mediated TRALI; if unavailable, rely on clinical criteria.

sections.p: Rapid respiratory deterioration can lead to severe ARDS and multi‑organ failure.
b: Progressive hypoxemia despite oxygen.
Need for invasive ventilation within hours.
Concurrent sepsis or severe anemia.

sections.p: Stop the transfusion immediately, then provide supportive care focused on oxygenation and hemodynamic stability.
b: High‑flow oxygen or CPAP; intubate if PaO2/FiO2 < 100 mmHg.
Fluid restriction; avoid diuretics unless volume overload suspected.
Consider corticosteroids only in refractory cases; not routine.
Notify blood bank; use male‑only plasma donors for future transfusions.

sections.p: Monitor respiratory status for 24‑48 h; educate patients and staff about donor selection.
b: Repeat chest imaging after 24 h to ensure resolution.
Implement male‑only plasma and low‑antibody donor policies.
Document reaction in transfusion safety system.

sections.p: Conditions that cause acute hypoxemia and infiltrates after transfusion.
b: Transfusion‑associated circulatory overload (TACO) – cardiogenic, high BNP.
Acute respiratory distress syndrome from sepsis or aspiration.
Anaphylactic transfusion reaction – bronchospasm, urticaria.

sections.p: Certain labs may appear normal despite severe injury.
b: BNP may be low even with mild cardiac strain, falsely pointing to TRALI.
Chest X‑ray can be initially normal; repeat if suspicion remains.
Antibody testing may be unavailable; clinical diagnosis must be used.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe shortness of breath with oxygen saturation < 90% after transfusion
Rapidly falling blood pressure or loss of consciousness
Need for mechanical ventilation within hours of transfusion

faq.q: How is TRALI different from TACO?
faq.a: TRALI is non‑cardiogenic, with normal BNP and no fluid overload; TACO shows elevated BNP and signs of volume excess.

faq.q: Can TRALI occur after any blood product?
faq.a: Yes, it has been reported with plasma, platelets, red cells, and whole blood.

faq.q: Is there a role for steroids?
faq.a: Routine steroids are not recommended; they may be tried only in refractory cases after other causes are excluded.

exam: List the diagnostic criteria for TRALI and explain how you would differentiate it from TACO.
Describe the pathophysiological ‘two‑hit’ model of TRALI.
Outline the immediate management steps for a patient who develops TRALI during transfusion.
